title: "Planning the development of a logistic risk model with imbsize"

  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Planning the development of a logistic risk model with imbsize}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A team plans a model for death within 14 days after acute ischaemic stroke, with 71 predictor columns. From
previous models it anticipates a C-statistic of 0.81 and a prevalence of 0.092.

```{r}
library(imbsize)
imbsize(cstatistic = 0.81, prevalence = 0.0916, parameters = 71, form = "closed")
```

The closed forms are immediate; `form = "exact"` (the default) solves the fixed-point equations and takes a few
seconds per method. C1 applies if the model will be used without recalibration, C2 if it will be recalibrated
(Platt scaling on leave-one-out scores). To meet the target in 90% of studies rather than on average:

```{r}
ss_c2(0.81, 0.0916, 71, method = "unweighted", assurance = 0.9, form = "closed")
```

The constants behind the closed forms:

```{r}
criteria_constants(0.81, 0.0916, "unweighted")
```

How the cost of rebalancing depends on the prevalence and the C-statistic:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(rebalancing_cost(c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9), c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)))
```

The criteria assume Gaussian predictors given the outcome and a correctly specified model. With mostly binary
predictors and rare categories they can recommend too few patients: add about 20%, or simulate on pilot
covariates. The criteria of Riley et al. on the optimism of R² and the precision of the overall risk still apply.
